investigations.name: Burning and Suppression of Solids – II
investigations.hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), BASS small flow duct (wind tunnel)
investigations.objective: Study ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction limits of solid fuels in low-velocity forced flow in microgravity, and begin to bridge the gap between the 1-g NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 and real material flammability in microgravity.

fuel.geometry: thin PMMA films, PMMA slabs (one- and two-sided), PMMA rods, PMMA spherical section, fabric strips
fuel.size: films 0.1–0.4 mm thick, slabs 1–5 mm thick, 1–2 cm wide; rods 1/4–1/2 in (6.35–12.7 mm) diameter

varied: ambient O2 concentration (N2 vitiation of the MSG working volume)
constant: pressure ~1 atm (MSG working volume; stated in NASA/TM-20210011385, not measured per test)
diagnostics: video camera with data overlay (fan, flow, radiometer)
investigations.resultSummary: About 130 flame tests on PMMA films, slabs, rods, fabrics and a candle in a small wind tunnel on the ISS, with O2 reduced below 21 % by nitrogen dilution. Flames were very sensitive to air flow between 0 and 5 cm/s and could survive at flows below 1 cm/s as dim blue flames that flare up when flow increases. Measured heat-release rates were mostly below 100 W.

keyFindings.text: Flames are quite sensitive to air flow speed in the range 0–5 cm/s and can be sustained at speeds below 1 cm/s, where they become dim, blue and stable; they can flare up quickly if the air flow suddenly increases.
BASS-II was the first ISS test to dilute the MSG working volume with N2, adding ambient O2 as a controlled variable.
Heat-release rates computed from O2 consumption were well below 100 W for most tests; the global equivalence ratio was fuel-rich (about 1.3 on average).
Hypothesis tested: with adequate ventilation, materials in microgravity burn as well as or better than in normal gravity, so the 1-g upward-burning test may not be conservative for space.

investigations.earthRelevance: Validated combustion models apply to wildfires, building fires and waste-to-energy combustion (PSI research impacts).

investigations.name: Burning and Suppression of Solids
investigations.hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), BASS flow duct (76 x 76 mm cross-section) with N2 suppression jet
investigations.objective: Bridge the gap between the 1-g NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, ground-based microgravity tests and real material flammability in microgravity, and assess how well an inert gaseous extinguishing agent (N2, similar to that used on ISS) puts out flames.

fuel.geometry: fabric strips, PMMA spheres and slabs, sheets, candles and wax slabs
fuel.size: 1–2 cm wide fabric strips; 1 and 2 cm PMMA spheres

varied: ambient O2 (some 2013 tests vitiated with N2)
constant: ISS cabin pressure (~0.97–1.0 atm per as-run matrix)
investigations.resultSummary: Over a hundred small-scale ISS tests burned fabrics, PMMA spheres and slabs and candles in a low-speed air flow, sometimes followed by an N2 jet to try to extinguish them. Flames were especially sensitive to flow in the 0–5 cm/s range; at the lowest flows they became dim and blue but could keep burning for a long time.

keyFindings.text: Microgravity flames were especially sensitive to air flow speed in the range 0–5 cm/s, and responded to flow changes with almost no delay.
Even the smallest acrylic-slab flames burned for over 5 minutes before self-extinguishing — a tiny flame could go undetected for a long time and flare up if convection increases.
Using N2 as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned ISS extinguishment techniques.

investigations.earthRelevance: Microgravity-validated combustion models feed back into terrestrial fire models (PSI research impacts).

investigations.name: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment – I
investigations.hardware: Saffire-I flow duct in the Cygnus cargo vehicle (after unberthing from ISS)
investigations.objective: Determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and compare low-g flammability limits with NASA's 1-g material screening test.

fuel.geometry: single large fabric sheet in a flow duct

investigations.resultSummary: The first intentionally large fire set inside an orbiting spacecraft: a 94 x 40.6 cm cotton-fiberglass sheet burned in a 20 cm/s air flow, once with and once against the flow. In concurrent spread the flame size stayed limited after ignition, unlike the accelerating upward fire seen on Earth.

keyFindings.text: The 94 x 40.6 cm sample was an order of magnitude larger than anything previously burned in microgravity.
In concurrent spread the flame size remained constrained after ignition — qualitatively different from Earth, where an upward-spreading flame on a sample this size accelerates and grows.
The flame in the large Saffire duct spread more slowly than in earlier small-tunnel microgravity tests, attributed to flow acceleration by hot-gas expansion in small tunnels — scale matters.

investigations.earthRelevance: Fire behaviour in small sealed volumes informs fire safety in mines, aircraft and submarines (PSI research impacts).

investigations.name: Spacecraft Fire Experiment – II
investigations.hardware: Saffire flow duct in the Cygnus pressurized cargo module
investigations.objective: Measure low-g flammability of several spacecraft materials at realistic scale and compare with NASA's 1-g material flammability screening test.

fuel.size: 5 cm x 29 cm each, 0.27–10 mm thick

investigations.resultSummary: Nine material samples were burned one after another in a Cygnus vehicle. Thin silicone did not sustain a flame in microgravity, while cotton-fiberglass fabric burned its full 29 cm length at 2.1–2.6 mm/s. Thick PMMA flames stayed anchored near the base, spreading far more slowly than the 1-g comparison.

keyFindings.text: Microgravity flame spread over SIBAL fabric in 20 cm/s concurrent flow was 2.1–2.6 mm/s, burning the full 29 cm sample (PSI test table).
Silicone samples ignited (80 W, 9.2 s) but had insignificant burn time in microgravity, while in the 1-g comparison the thinnest (0.27 mm) silicone sample burned completely.
Reducing pressure slows concurrent flame spread over thick PMMA toward the microgravity value; a mixed-convection correlation extrapolated to low pressure predicts the Saffire II spread rate.

investigations.earthRelevance: Low-pressure ground tests may approximate untested gravity levels for thick and thin solids (NTRS 20200000557).

investigations.name: Flame Extinguishment Experiment
investigations.hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA)
investigations.objective: Map flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity, measure the effectiveness of gaseous suppressants (CO2, He) and determine the limiting oxygen index (LOI) as a function of pressure and suppressant concentration.
diagnostics: droplet and flame imaging (droplet diameter history, burning rate, extinction diameter)
investigations.resultSummary: 274 droplet tests burned methanol and heptane in mixtures of O2, N2, CO2 and He at 0.7–3 atm. Each test ended in flame extinction, droplet disruption or burning to completion. The data give the oxygen level below which these fuels stop burning and how much CO2 or helium is needed.

keyFindings.text: The limiting oxygen index for methanol droplets in O2–N2–CO2 and O2–N2–He mixtures is around 12–13 % O2 by volume.
Droplets of ~1.5–4 mm captured both diffusive extinction (too little residence time) and radiative extinction (too much heat loss).
FLEX was designed to assess fire suppressants in microgravity and the effect of candidate crew exploration atmospheres on fire suppression.

investigations.earthRelevance: Suppressant effectiveness results can inform less harmful fire-suppression systems; relevant to submarines and high-altitude aircraft (PSI research impacts).

investigations.name: Cool Flames Investigation
investigations.hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA)
investigations.objective: Study low-temperature 'cool flame' droplet combustion of n-dodecane and n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures at 0.5–5 atm, including helium dilution, and relate droplet size, pressure and extinction.
investigations.resultSummary: 79 unique droplet tests explored how dodecane droplets keep burning after the visible hot flame goes out, sustained by an invisible low-temperature 'cool flame'. Hot- and cool-flame burning rates and extinction diameters are tabulated for most tests.

keyFindings.text: Cool-flame-supported quasi-steady droplet burning was first observed on the ISS; these flames are not visible to the naked eye.

investigations.hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), Comparative Soot Diagnostic hardware with aging chamber
investigations.objective: Measure the size of smoke particles produced by overheated spacecraft materials in microgravity and relate them to smoke generation and transport, to evaluate and design spacecraft smoke detectors.

fuel.geometry: heated samples in a smoke-generation tube

conditions.assumptionNote: assumption: ISS cabin air (21% O2, 101.3 kPa). The test ran in the MSG work volume on the ISS (SAME Final Science Report p.20-21; SAME-R Final Report p.9: smoke 'diffused out of the inlet into the MSG volume'); neither report states O2 or pressure or mentions a purge or backfill gas (N2 was added only to dilute the sampled aerosol). MSG work-volume N2 dilution was first used later, by BASS-II (NTRS 20150019858).

diagnostics: DustTrak aerosol monitor and ionization detector (Commercial Diagnostic Enclosure)
investigations.resultSummary: Spacecraft materials were overheated on the ISS to produce smoke, which was aged and measured by detectors and particle samplers. The hypothesis was that low-gravity smoke particles grow larger than on Earth, which could change how smoke detectors respond.

keyFindings.text: Hypothesis: without buoyant flow, smoke particles grow larger in microgravity (longer residence time near the source), which may stop some detectors from alarming.
All current spacecraft smoke detectors were designed from normal-gravity data; earlier shuttle experiments saw larger particles in low gravity in some cases.
After SAME, the TEM grids returned to the ground were contaminated with foreign particles and unusable, which motivated the SAME-R reflight.

investigations.earthRelevance: Better smoke detectors for extreme environments such as submarines and underwater laboratories (PSI research impacts).

investigations.name: ACME – Burning Rate Emulator
investigations.hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME modular hardware, porous flat burner with heat-flux gauge
investigations.objective: Use a gas burner that emulates condensed (solid/liquid) fuels to find the conditions for steady burning in a quiescent microgravity ambient, including candidate spacecraft atmospheres (21 % O2 at 14.7 psia, 26.5 % at 10.2 psia, 34 % at 8.2 psia).
diagnostics: heat-flux gauge and burner surface temperature
investigations.resultSummary: A gas-fed burner emulating solids like PMMA and nylon burned in still air on the ISS. In elevated-oxygen atmospheres being considered for future spacecraft the flames kept burning without any air flow, whereas at 21 % O2 they self-extinguished in a short time.

keyFindings.text: Quasi-steady burning of emulated condensed materials (e.g. PMMA, nylon) was observed in microgravity without air flow — even though stopping ventilation is a standard step in fighting spacecraft fires.
Sustained burning without air flow was seen in elevated-O2 atmospheres considered for future spacecraft, whereas flames at 21 % O2 self-extinguished quickly.
Results suggest NASA may want to increase use of its cone-calorimeter Test 2, which can measure the material properties that govern these microgravity flames.

investigations.earthRelevance: Links microgravity flammability to cone-calorimeter (NASA-STD-6001 Test 2) material properties (PSI research impacts).

investigations.hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME modular hardware, spherical porous burner
investigations.objective: Determine the conditions for steady cool diffusion flames of gaseous fuels on spherical porous burners, for normal and inverse flames over a broad range of stoichiometric mixture fraction, adiabatic flame temperature and flow rate.

fuel.geometry: spherical porous burner (normal: fuel out; inverse: oxidizer out)

investigations.resultSummary: Spherical gas flames on the ISS were used to look for cool flames and to map when flames ignite, self-extinguish or burn until the fuel is cut. Inverse flames reached the highest oxygen levels flown in these data (oxidizer stream up to 85 % O2), but they are gas flames, not burning materials.

keyFindings.text: Hypotheses include demonstrating, for the first time, steady cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners, inverse cool diffusion flames, and cool flames over a wide range of Zst, Tad and pressure.
ACME's six investigations of gaseous non-premixed flames ran on the ISS from Nov 2017 to Feb 2022; three of them used porous spherical burners giving a nominally one-dimensional flame.

investigations.earthRelevance: Cool-flame kinetics could enable ultra-lean, higher-efficiency engines (PSI research impacts).

investigations.name: ACME – Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
investigations.hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME coflow and gas-jet burners with high-voltage mesh electrode (up to 10 kV)
investigations.objective: Understand how electric fields act on laminar diffusion flames in microgravity: voltage vs chemi-ion current, dynamic flame response, soot formation and stabilized near-limit lifted flames.
diagnostics: filtered spectral imaging (chemiluminescence, soot volume fraction)
investigations.resultSummary: Methane and ethylene flames on the ISS were exposed to electric fields of either polarity to study ion-driven flows, soot and flame stability without buoyancy. It is a fundamental combustion study, not a fire-safety test.

keyFindings.text: Microgravity isolates electric-field (ion-driven convection) effects from buoyancy; voltage–current curves reveal ion-driven convection effects.
Electric-field control of flames may reduce pollutant and soot emissions in terrestrial combustion; the work is not aimed at a space application.

investigations.earthRelevance: Electric-field flame control may lower soot and pollutant emissions and improve combustion efficiency (PSI research impacts).

investigations.name: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment
investigations.hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), SPICE flow duct with nozzles
investigations.objective: Find the laminar smoke point (onset of soot emission) of non-buoyant gas-jet flames in co-flowing air and how burner diameter, co-flow velocity and fuel affect it.

fuel.geometry: round jet nozzles in co-flowing air

constant: cabin air co-flow (nominal 21 % O2, 101 kPa per SPICE Final Report)
diagnostics: still and video cameras (flame length, smoke point)
investigations.resultSummary: 526 small gas-jet flames were studied in the glovebox to find when they begin to emit soot. Soot governs flame heat emission, so the data help predict fire spread and support material flammability criteria.

keyFindings.text: Soot dominates heat emitted from flames in both normal gravity and microgravity fires; controlling it matters for preventing fire spread.
In total 526 flames were studied, with co-flow velocities from 5.4 to 65 cm/s and three burner diameters.

investigations.earthRelevance: Better soot control for jet engines and power-generation boilers (NTRS 20090014827).

From it: extra.flameLengthMm (luminous flame length from video, mm), extra.nikonFlameHeightMm, extra.smokeHeightFlag ('Smoke Height' Y/N column), extra.flagSH / extra.flagLO (columns headed 'SH ?' / 'LO ?', undocumented — LO is probably lift-off), extra.comment.

smokePointLengthMm = luminous flame length at the smoke point (mm) from the curated sheet 'Smoke Point Datasheet' of 'PSI-107_Raw Data_SmokePointReview-0g-3.xlsx' (55 ISS smoke points; the SPICE Final Report Table 1 counts 52). Attached to 53 PSI rows: same day, nozzle and ignition time, then the fuel/air setting nearest to the review sheet's (the review recomputed fuel rates with corrected meter factors; its values are kept in extra.smokePointAirCmS / smokePointFuelRateSccm); no PSI row with that ignition time for E16-1, 75P16-3. All other rows are not at their smoke point -> null.

Outcome: 'not_applicable' for every row. SPICE deliberately ignited every flame, so 'burned' would be a by-design constant, not a flammability result; SPICE rows are therefore excluded from burn/no-burn estimates and backtests (blow-off comments are kept in outcomeRaw). SPICE's natural per-row result is the smoke point (sooting vs non-sooting); the Final Report notes 'All smoke point flames were attached to the burner, i.e., not lifted'.

investigations.resultSummary: On 12 test days in 2012, methane, ethylene and other gas flames were photographed in co-flowing air to study lift-off, blow-out and soot. Microgravity flames were longer and sootier than their 1-g counterparts.

keyFindings.text: Microgravity sooting CH4 flames had lower soot temperatures and higher soot volume fractions than normal-gravity flames, with soot shifting from the centerline to the wings.
Non-buoyant luminous flame lengths are proportional to fuel mass flow rate and noticeably longer than 1-g flames; buoyancy narrows the flame by radially inward convection.

claims.text: BASS aimed to begin bridging the gap between the normal-gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 method, ground-based microgravity tests and actual material flammability in microgravity.

sourceRef.quote: Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity.

claims.text: BASS assessed how well an inert gaseous extinguishing agent, similar to the one used on ISS, puts out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating and flow.

sourceRef.quote: Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow.

claims.text: BASS burned custom fabric samples of 75% cotton / 25% fiberglass by mass, plus Nomex fabric and Ultem.

sourceRef.quote: Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) measuring were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem.

claims.text: In BASS the air flow along the sample reached up to 40 cm/s and could be opposed or concurrent to flame spread; the flow duct cross-section was 76 mm x 76 mm.

sourceRef.quote: The samples were placed in a small flow duct (76 mm x 76 mm cross section) that allowed for airflow across the fabric.

claims.text: Current NASA spacecraft material selection (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) segregates materials on 1-g behavior without considering low-gravity effects.

sourceRef.quote: Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects.

claims.text: Using nitrogen as the flame suppressant in BASS links the results directly to current and planned extinguishment techniques.

sourceRef.quote: Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques.

claims.text: BASS microgravity flames were especially sensitive to air flow speed in the 0 to 5 cm/s range.

sourceRef.quote: Microgravity flames were found to be especially sensitive to air flow speed in the range 0 to 5 cms.

claims.text: At the lowest flow speeds tested in BASS (below 1 cm/s) flames became dim blue and very stable and, with small heat loss, could burn for a long time.

sourceRef.quote: At the lowest speeds examined (less than 1 cms) all the flames tended to become dim blue and very stable. However, heat loss at these very low convective rates is small so the flames can burn for a long time.

claims.text: Even the smallest BASS flames on acrylic slabs burned for over 5 minutes before self-extinguishing, so a tiny flame might go undetected for a long time.

sourceRef.quote: Only the smallest flames burning acrylic slabs appeared to be adversely influenced by solid conductive heat loss, but even these burned for over 5 minutes before self-extinguishing. This has implications for spacecraft fire safety since a tiny flame might be undetected for a long time.

claims.text: A small, stable microgravity flame can flare up if air convection is suddenly increased or if it spreads into another fuel source.

sourceRef.quote: the danger is that it might flare up if the air convection is suddenly increased or if the flame spreads into another fuel source

claims.text: In some BASS tests a jet of nitrogen was introduced to try to extinguish the flame.

sourceRef.quote: In some cases, a jet of nitrogen was introduced to attempt to extinguish the flame.

claims.text: At moderate flow speeds (about 1 to 5 cm/s) the flame keeps heating the solid fuel, giving an increasingly strong, luminous flame over time.

sourceRef.quote: At moderate flow speeds (between about 1 and 5 cms) the flame continually heats the solid fuel resulting in an increasing fuel temperature, higher rate of fuel vaporization, and a stronger, more luminous flame as time progresses.

claims.text: BASS-II objective: study ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction limits of solid fuels in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity.

sourceRef.quote: Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity.

claims.text: BASS-II aimed to begin bridging the gap between NASA-STD-6001 Test #1, ground-based microgravity tests and actual microgravity flammability.

sourceRef.quote: Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity.

claims.text: In BASS-II oxygen was varied only below 21% by adding nitrogen, and the wind tunnel imposed airflow up to 40 cm/s.

sourceRef.quote: Main variables are airflow speed and oxygen concentration (oxygen varied below 21% by adding nitrogen).

claims.text: BASS-II tests the hypothesis that, with adequate ventilation, materials burn as well or better in microgravity than in normal gravity under otherwise identical conditions.

sourceRef.quote: BASS–II tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity

claims.text: NASA's upward-burning 1-g material test is considered worst case on Earth but may not be conservative for flammability in space.

sourceRef.quote:
NASA tests and controls materials from a flammability perspective using an upward burning test in normal gravity, which is considered to be the worst-case geometry for
flammability of the material on Earth. However, it may not be conservative for flammability in space.

claims.text: BASS-II flames are quite sensitive to air flow speed in the 0 to 5 cm/s range and can be sustained below 1 cm/s as dim blue, stable flames.

sourceRef.quote: The flames are quite sensitive to air flow speed in the range 0 to 5 cms. They can be sustained at very low flow speeds of less than 1 cms, when they become dim blue and stable.

claims.text: Very-low-flow dim blue flames are not particularly dangerous but can flare up quickly with a sudden increase in air flow speed.

sourceRef.quote: In this state they are not particularly dangerous from a fire safety perspective, but they can flare up quickly with a sudden increase in air flow speed.

claims.text: Including BASS-I, well over one hundred tests were run across geometries, flow speeds and oxygen concentrations; the BASS-II tunnel could impose flows up to 53 cm/s.

sourceRef.quote: Including earlier BASS-I results, well over one hundred tests have been conducted of the various samples in the different geometries, flow speeds, and oxygen concentrations.

claims.text: Across both BASS and BASS-II concurrent-flow SIBAL cotton-fiberglass tests (1.2 and 2.2 cm wide, 16-21% O2), low-speed quenching extinction occurred at 1 to 5 cm/s with higher quench speeds in lower oxygen.
claims.conditionsScope: BASS and BASS-II combined ISS MSG concurrent-flow SIBAL fabric tests; 1.2 & 2.2 cm wide, 10 cm long; 16-21% O2, 1-40 cm/s
limitations: Applies jointly to BASS and BASS-II SIBAL concurrent-flow datasets rather than BASS-II in isolation.

sourceRef.quote: As a part of the NASA BASS and BASS-II experimental projects aboard the International Space Station, flame growth, spread and extinction over a composite cotton-fiberglass fabric blend (referred to as the SIBAL fabric) were studied in low-speed concurrent forced flows. The tests were conducted in a small flow duct within the Microgravity Science Glovebox. The fuel samples measured 1.2 and 2.2 cm wide and 10 cm long. Ambient oxygen was varied from 21% down to 16% and flow speed from 40 cm/s down to 1 cm/s. A small flame resulted at low flow, enabling us to observe the entire history of flame development including ignition, flame growth, steady spread (in some cases) and decay at the end of the sample. In addition, by decreasing flow velocity during some of the tests, low-speed flame quenching extinction limits were found as a function of oxygen percentage. The quenching speeds were found to be between 1 and 5 cm/s with higher speed in lower oxygen atmosphere.
sourceRef.context: BASS and BASS-II combined ISS MSG concurrent-flow SIBAL fabric tests; 1.2 & 2.2 cm wide, 10 cm long; 16-21% O2, 1-40 cm/s

claims.text: SIBAL fabric tests varied ambient oxygen from 21% down to 16% and flow from 40 cm/s down to 1 cm/s.

sourceRef.quote: Ambient oxygen was varied from 21% down to 16% and flow speed from 40 cm/s down to 1 cm/s.

claims.text: Twenty-four concurrent-flow tests on cast PMMA rods mapped flammability limits as a function of oxygen and flow speed, finding both blowoff and quenching limits.

sourceRef.quote: Twenty-four concurrent-flow tests were performed, focusing on finding flammability limits as a function of oxygen and flow speed.

claims.text: Quenching of PMMA rod flames occurred when the flow became too weak for the flame to offset conduction and radiation heat losses.

sourceRef.quote: Quenching was observed when the flow became sufficiently weak that the flame could no longer provide adequate heat flux to compensate for the heat losses (conduction into the rod and radiation).

claims.text: On the blowoff branch the PMMA-rod flammability boundary depends linearly on oxygen concentration and stretch rate.

sourceRef.quote: For the blowoff branch, the boundary exhibits a linear dependence on oxygen concentration and stretch rate

claims.text: Most BASS-II tests had heat release rates well below 100 W (from oxygen consumption, 13.1 kJ per gram O2).

sourceRef.quote: The results showed that most of the tests had heat release rates well below 100 W.

claims.text: BASS-II was the first ISS experiment to dilute the glovebox working volume with gaseous N2 to reduce oxygen.

sourceRef.quote: For the first time on ISS, BASS–II utilized MSG working volume dilution with gaseous N2.

claims.text: The global equivalence ratio of BASS-II tests was estimated as fuel rich, 1.3 on average.

sourceRef.quote: the global equivalence ratio for the tests is estimated to be fuel rich, 1.3 on average using mass loss and O2 consumption data

claims.text: Normal-gravity blowoff limits for PMMA rods (0.635-3.81 cm, 14-18% O2) compare favorably with BASS-II when buoyant stretch and blockage are accounted for.

sourceRef.quote: These blowoff limits compare favorably with the BASS-II results when the buoyant stretch is included and the flow is corrected by considering the blockage factor of the fuel.

claims.text: A proposed new 1-g upward flame spread test extrapolates the linear blowoff boundary to zero stretch to estimate microgravity flammability limits, which current methods cannot do.

sourceRef.quote: We describe a new normal gravity 'upward flame spread test' method which extrapolates the linear blowoff boundary to the zero stretch limit in order to resolve microgravity flammability limits-something current methods cannot do.

claims.text: In 1-g the PMMA rod blowoff boundary is linear, with oxygen concentration directly proportional to flow speed.

sourceRef.quote: the normal gravity blowoff boundary for this axisymmetric rod geometry is determined to be linear, with oxygen concentration directly proportional to flow speed

claims.text: Saffire-I burned a SIBAL (75% cotton / 25% fiberglass) sample about 0.94 m long and 0.4 m wide.

sourceRef.quote: The sample was approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide, simulating a large piece of flammable fabric.

claims.text: Saffire-I was conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s.

sourceRef.quote: Saffire-I was conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s.

claims.text: Saffire objectives: determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and compare low-g flammability limits with NASA's 1-g screening test.

sourceRef.quote:
(1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal
gravity material flammability screening test.

claims.text: Saffire hypothesis: because fire behaves very differently in reduced gravity, designing spacecraft fire safety from terrestrial fires and standards carries inherent risk.

sourceRef.quote: the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty

claims.text: Saffire was the first test of spacecraft fires at a scale relevant to real spacecraft.

sourceRef.quote: The Saffire Experiment represents the first test of spacecraft fires at a scale relevant to real spacecraft.

claims.text: Downloaded data from the Saffire series resolved whether flame growth reaches a steady size and demonstrated that enclosure size around the sample affects flame spread more than anticipated.
claims.conditionsScope: Saffire series (Cygnus microgravity duct across early Saffire flights)
limitations: Source abstract ntrs-20180005168 summarizes the Saffire series broadly rather than Saffire-I alone; note verbatim typographical phrasing ('show resolved').

sourceRef.quote: The downloaded test data show resolved the question of whether flame growth will achieve a steady size and demonstrated that the size of the enclosure surrounding the sample has more impact on the flame spread than anticipated.
sourceRef.context: Saffire series (Cygnus microgravity duct across early Saffire flights)

claims.text: Spacecraft fire spread and growth cannot be expected to scale linearly from small-scale test data.

sourceRef.quote: The spread and growth of a fire, combined with its interactions with the vehicle cannot be expected to scale linearly from small-scale test data

claims.text: Before Saffire, microgravity fire experiments were limited to samples of order 10 cm in length and width or smaller.

sourceRef.quote: The major constraint has been the size of the sample, with prior experiments limited to samples of the order of 10 cm in length and width or smaller.

claims.text: The lack of large-scale data forces spacecraft designers to base fire safety designs on 1-g understanding of flame spread, detection and suppression.

sourceRef.quote: This lack of experimental data forces spacecraft designers to base their designs and safety precautions on 1-g understanding of flame spread, fire detection, and suppression.

claims.text: Pre-flight 2015 Saffire plans scheduled Saffire-1 and Saffire-3 as meter-scale flame spread tests burned to completion inside the Cygnus pressurized volume.
claims.conditionsScope: 2015 pre-flight experimental design for Saffire-1 and Saffire-3 (Cygnus)
limitations: Derived from a 2015 future-tense pre-flight poster (ntrs-20150000894); post-flight outcomes must be verified in Saffire-I/III telemetry rather than this plan.

sourceRef.quote: On two flights (Saffire-1 and Saffire-3), the experiment will consist of a flame spread test involving a meter-scale sample ignited in the pressurized volume of the spacecraft and allowed to burn to completion while measurements are made.
sourceRef.context: 2015 pre-flight experimental design for Saffire-1 and Saffire-3 (Cygnus)

claims.text: Low-gravity fire behaviour differs from normal gravity in flammability limits, ignition delay, flame spread, flame colour and structure.

sourceRef.quote: the work conducted to date has shown that fire behaviour in low-gravity is very different from that in normal-gravity, with differences observed for flammability limits, ignition delay, flame spread behaviour, flame colour and flame structure

claims.text: The Saffire project's overall objective is to reduce the uncertainty and risk in designing spacecraft fire safety systems for NASA exploration missions.

sourceRef.quote: The overall objective of this project is to reduce the uncertainty and risk associated with the design of spacecraft fire safety systems for NASA's exploration missions.

claims.text: Saffire tests are fully automated in Cygnus after it unberths from ISS, with data downlinked before reentry.

sourceRef.quote: The tests will be fully automated with the data downlinked at the conclusion of the test and before the Cygnus vehicle reenters the atmosphere.

claims.text: Saffire-II carried a 9-sample card (5 cm x 29 cm each) adding SIBAL, silicone, structural PMMA, flat PMMA, and PMMA with Nomex.
claims.conditionsScope: Saffire-II Cygnus flight hardware and 9-sample card configuration
limitations: Note PSI-99 OCR artifact ('Saffire-1I', 'structure PMMA') in verbatim quote.

sourceRef.quote: As a follow on to the Saffire-I investigation, the Saffire-II investigation added more samples including SIBAL, silicone, structure PMMA, flat PMMA, and PMMA with Nomex. The Saffire-1I flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct. Air is drawn through the flow duct by fans located at the top of the duct with flow straighteners at the bottom of the experiment module. Saffire-II has a sample card that contains 9 samples, each 5 cm x 29 cm.
sourceRef.context: Saffire-II Cygnus flight hardware and 9-sample card configuration

claims.text: Saffire-II added more samples including SIBAL, silicone, structure PMMA, flat PMMA and PMMA with Nomex.

sourceRef.quote: the Saffire-II investigation added more samples including SIBAL, silicone, structure PMMA, flat PMMA, and PMMA with Nomex

claims.text: Depending on material, Saffire-II used 20 or 30 cm/s air flow, either concurrent or opposed.

sourceRef.quote: Depending on the sample material, the Saffire-II was conducted at an air flow velocity of either 20 or 30 cm/s, the flow being either concurrent or opposed.

claims.text: Saffire-2 was designed to test 9 smaller (5 x 30 cm) samples to evaluate NASA's material flammability screening tests.

missions.label: International Space Station (cabin)
missions.notes: Sea-level air: NASA's OCHMO technical brief states the ISS cabin is 'typically maintained at 14.7 psia with 21% O2' (14.7 psia = 101.3 kPa). Ventilation band 5-20 cm/s is an EMBER engineering assumption: NASA sources describe spacecraft ventilation as 'of the order of 0.1 m/s' (NTRS 19990053973) and 'a few centimeters per second' (NTRS 20050199446); NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 2 [V2 6107] only requires circulation that prevents CO2 and thermal pockets, without a numeric velocity.

NTRS 20050199446 – TIGER Burned Brightly in JAMIC (ventilation: a few cm/s)

missions.label: Crew capsule in transit (Orion-class)
missions.notes: Modeled as sea-level air like ISS. We did not find a NASA page that states Orion's nominal Artemis cabin O2/pressure numerically, so the values are an assumption. Context from NASA: Orion was once designed for 'up to 30% oxygen at a pressure of 10.2 psia for lunar missions' and its materials are certified at 30% O2 / 10.2 psia; at 14.7 psia the cabin O2 'cannot be set higher than 25.6%' without potentially invalidating that certification (NTRS 20090012334). Shuttle also flew 10.2 psia / 26.5% O2 during staged EVA prep (NTRS 20240003211).

missions.label: Lunar surface habitat (exploration atmosphere)
missions.notes: NASA's recommended exploration atmosphere for EVA-intensive lunar surface habitats: 8.2 psia (56.5 kPa) / 34% O2 (revised from 8.0 psia / 32%). NASA notes the final specification is still being evaluated and that fire management in this oxygen-enriched atmosphere is an open challenge; a 2026 NASA paper reports a team recommendation of an 'alternate vehicle atmosphere' for early surface missions (NTRS 20260002050) and NASA chamber tests used an 'alternate exploration atmosphere' of 66.2 kPa / 28.5% O2 (NTRS 20240013238). Ventilation band is an assumption (see iss).

NASA has not published a rover cabin atmosphere specification that we could find, so this is a design scenario, not a NASA rover spec. earth.title: Lightweight firefighter air tanks (SCBA)
earth.summary: NASA Johnson Space Center and Scott Aviation developed a lighter firefighter breathing-air backpack: about 20 lb for a 30-minute supply (13 lb less than conventional tanks), pressurized at 4,500 psi, built from an aluminum liner wrapped in resin-impregnated glass fibers.
earth.quote: New backpack system weighs only 20 pounds for 30 minute air supply, 13 pounds less than conventional firefighting tanks.
earth.linkNote: Heritage spinoff from spacecraft pressure-vessel technology; not derived from a PSI combustion investigation.

earth.title: Incipient fire detector from the Space Shuttle
earth.summary: The Brunswick Incipient Fire Detector, first used in Space Shuttle orbiters, samples air for combustion particles and can tell them apart from dust, so it gives fewer false alarms and can signal a fire before flame and smoke appear. SAME and SAME-R carry this line forward: they measured how smoke particle sizes change in microgravity to set the requirements for next-generation spacecraft smoke detectors, and NASA notes the resulting detectors could also serve submarines and underwater laboratories.
earth.quote: Fire detector represents an advancement over commercially available smoke detectors in that it senses and signals the presence of a fire condition before appearance of flame and smoke.

earth.title: New technology for fire attire (Project FIRES, PBI fabric)
earth.summary: Project FIRES, sponsored by NASA and FEMA's U.S. Fire Administration and managed by Marshall Space Flight Center, applied lightweight, fire-resistant, heat-protective materials developed for spacesuits and spacecraft to firefighter turnout gear. After the Apollo 1 fire NASA pushed PBI fiber for flight suits; PBI later became the PBI Gold outer shell used in firefighter gear. This is the same material-flammability question BASS, BASS-II and Saffire study in microgravity.
earth.quote: A major focus of the effort involves application to the FIRES ensemble of lightweight, fire-resistant, heat-protective materials originally developed for use in astronauts' space suits or in spacecraft components which require thermal protection.
earth.linkNote: Thematic link (material flammability), not a direct technology transfer from these experiments.

earth.title: Fine-water-mist fire extinguisher
earth.summary: NASA Glenn and ADA Technologies (SBIR funding over about 10 years) built a fine-water-mist portable extinguisher for the ISS to replace CO2 units: 6 lb of water and 1.2 lb of nitrogen, working in any orientation. Its zero-leak valve maker (Doering) now sells the same class of valve to industry. FLEX measured how gaseous suppressants (CO2, He) and exploration atmospheres affect extinction in microgravity, the evidence base for choosing spacecraft suppressants.
earth.quote: A fine-water-mist portable fire extinguisher made the most sense: it wouldn’t cause damage to structures or require special cleanup procedures and would meet the other criteria.
earth.linkNote: FLEX studied gaseous suppressants, not water mist; the link is the shared question of what to put out a spacecraft fire with.

earth.title: Wool filters for fire respirators
earth.summary: Work to extend the life of the respirator Orion crews would wear during a cabin fire led New Zealand company Lanaco to improve its wool filter line for firefighters on Earth. NASA notes Orion crews could have to stay longer in a fire-contaminated cabin than ISS crews.
earth.quote: A New Zealand-based company’s work to help astronauts fight fires in case of an anomaly on the Orion spacecraft is already informing its line of wool filters for firefighters on Earth.

earth.title: Less harmful fire suppressants (FLEX)

history.title: Apollo 1 pad fire
history.summary: During a preflight test of Apollo 204 (AS-204), a fire swept through the command module and killed Virgil Grissom, Edward White and Roger Chaffee. NASA then sharply limited the amount and location of combustible materials in the command module and flight suits, pursued fire-resistant fabrics such as PBI, and changed ground procedures from 100% O2 to a 60% O2 / 40% N2 mixture.
history.quote: Astronauts Virgil Grissom, Edward White and Roger Chaffee lost their lives when a fire swept through the command module.
history.lesson: Oxygen-rich cabin atmospheres plus flammable materials are the core risk EMBER's oxygen-limit evidence addresses.

history.title: Apollo 13 oxygen tank failure
history.summary: Oxygen tank no. 2 in the service module failed from combustion inside the tank. The Apollo 13 Review Board found the most probable cause was ignition of Teflon wire insulation on the fan motor wires by electric arcs; the insulation had been damaged when heater thermostatic switches failed closed during ground detanking. It showed that materials normally thought safe can burn in pure, high-pressure oxygen.
history.quote: The cause of the combustion was most probably the ignition of Teflon wire insulation on the fan motor wires, caused by electric arcs in this wiring.
history.lesson: Ignition sources and materials in oxygen systems need flammability testing at the real oxygen condition.

history.title: Fire aboard space station Mir (oxygen candle)
history.summary: With six crew aboard, a solid-fuel oxygen generator canister (lithium perchlorate 'candle') in Mir's Kvant-1 module ignited and shot a flame about three feet long. It blocked access to one of the two Soyuz escape vehicles and filled the modules with smoke. The crew put the fire out; life support cleared the smoke over several hours. Lessons were carried into ISS design and operations.
history.quote: The searing flame, lasting several minutes, not only cut off access to one of the two Soyuz escape vehicles but also filled the station’s modules with smoke.
history.lesson: Smoke spreads through the whole station and escape routes can be cut off, which is why detection (SAME) and suppression (FLEX) data matter. NASA dates the fire Feb. 24, 1997; some accounts give Feb. 23 (US time).

sources.label: NASA History – 25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir

history.title: Saffire: setting real fires in an empty spacecraft
history.summary: Because earlier microgravity fire tests used samples of only about 10 cm, NASA ran Saffire inside uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicles after they left the ISS. Saffire-I and -III burned a large cotton-fiberglass sheet (about 0.94 m x 0.4 m) and Saffire-II burned nine Test 1-sized samples. It was the first test of spacecraft fires at a realistic scale. Results showed that the size of the enclosure around a fire matters more than expected. Saffire IV-VI followed with fires up to 10 kW.
history.quote: The Saffire Experiment represents the first test of spacecraft fires at a scale relevant to real spacecraft.
history.lesson: Fire growth does not scale linearly from small samples, so large-scale data are needed to validate material limits and fire models.

history.title: First extended burns in simulated lunar gravity (LUCI)
history.summary: The Lunar Combustion Investigation spun a Blue Origin New Shepard rocket to create lunar gravity and ran the first combustion tests longer than 25 s at lunar g, burning a cotton-fiberglass fabric and a 4 mm PMMA rod in air. It leads into FM2 (Flammability of Materials on the Moon), planned to launch in late 2026. This is the partial-gravity data PSI does not yet contain.
history.quote: These are the first-ever, extended-duration (greater than 25 seconds) combustion tests performed in simulated Lunar gravity.
history.lesson: Partial-gravity flammability is only now being measured; EMBER marks lunar and Mars answers as 1 g / 0 g bounds, not measurements.

extractionEval.method: Concept section 8, check 2. Claims in claims.json were produced in the LLM-extractor role (extractedBy 'llm') from cached NTRS abstracts and PSI investigation records (pipeline/content/cache/sources.json). A systematic sample of 36 (every 4th claim: c-0001, c-0005, ... c-0141) was re-checked by a separate manual-annotator pass: the cited source was re-read, a gold statement written from the source alone, and the LLM statement graded correct (fully supported, right investigation), partial (true but with an attribution, tense or quote-coverage problem) or wrong (contradicted or unsupported). Programmatic check: every quote was searched verbatim in the cached source text (whitespace/quote-mark normalized; also exact substring): 36/36 sampled and 145/145 of all claims matched (100%). Verbatim quotes do not guarantee a correct claim - all partial verdicts below have verbatim quotes. Caveats: the annotator is the same model family as the extractor (not an independent human), so agreement is likely optimistic; before this evaluation, 2 non-sampled claims from NTRS 20150018397 were re-attributed from CFI to FLEX after review.

items.goldText: Objective 1 of BASS: begin to bridge the gap between NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 (1 g), ground-based microgravity tests and real microgravity flammability.
items.llmText: BASS aimed to begin bridging the gap between the normal-gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 method, ground-based microgravity tests and actual material flammability in microgravity.
items.note: Matches PSI-26 objective 1.

items.goldText: PSI-26 states current spacecraft material selection uses NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, which sorts materials by 1-g behavior with no consideration of low-gravity effects.
items.llmText: Current NASA spacecraft material selection (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) segregates materials on 1-g behavior without considering low-gravity effects.

items.goldText: The smallest acrylic-slab flames were hurt by conductive heat loss yet still burned >5 min before self-extinguishing; authors note a tiny flame might go undetected for a long time.
items.llmText: Even the smallest BASS flames on acrylic slabs burned for over 5 minutes before self-extinguishing, so a tiny flame might go undetected for a long time.
items.note: Faithful; the claim omits the 'conductive heat loss' qualifier but does not change the meaning.

items.goldText: BASS-II objective 1: study ignition, flame growth, spread and extinction limits of solid fuels in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity.
items.llmText: BASS-II objective: study ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction limits of solid fuels in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity.

items.goldText: NASA's 1-g upward-burning test is considered the worst-case geometry on Earth but may not be conservative for flammability in space (BASS-II hypothesis section).
items.llmText: NASA's upward-burning 1-g material test is considered worst case on Earth but may not be conservative for flammability in space.
items.note: The source frames this inside the hypothesis section; claim keeps it as a statement of NASA's own concern, which is acceptable.

items.goldText: SIBAL fabric (1.2/2.2 cm x 10 cm) in low-speed concurrent flow: quenching speeds 1-5 cm/s, higher quench speed in lower O2 (21% to 16% tested). Work is part of both BASS and BASS-II.
items.llmText: For the SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric in concurrent flow, low-speed quenching extinction occurred at 1 to 5 cm/s, with higher quench speed at lower oxygen.
items.note: Numbers correct, but the source says the tests belong to 'the NASA BASS and BASS-II experimental projects'; attributing only to BASS-II loses half the provenance.

items.goldText: For PMMA rods in concurrent flow, the blowoff branch of the flammability boundary is linear in oxygen concentration and stretch rate.
items.llmText: On the blowoff branch the PMMA-rod flammability boundary depends linearly on oxygen concentration and stretch rate.

items.goldText: Ground (1 g) PMMA rods 0.635-3.81 cm at 14-18% O2: blowoff limits agree with BASS-II microgravity results once buoyant stretch and blockage factor are included.
items.llmText: Normal-gravity blowoff limits for PMMA rods (0.635-3.81 cm, 14-18% O2) compare favorably with BASS-II when buoyant stretch and blockage are accounted for.
items.note: Claim correctly identifies these as normal-gravity tests compared against BASS-II.

items.goldText: Saffire-I: SIBAL sample, air flow velocity 20 cm/s.
items.llmText: Saffire-I was conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s.

items.goldText: Saffire downlinked data resolved whether flame growth reaches a steady size; the enclosure size around the sample affected spread more than expected.
items.llmText: Saffire data resolved whether flame growth reaches a steady size and showed the enclosure around the sample affects flame spread more than anticipated.
items.note: Content correct, but the 2018 abstract summarizes the Saffire series, not Saffire-I alone; the inv attribution is an inference. The source sentence itself is ungrammatical ('data show resolved').

items.goldText: 2015 plan: Saffire-1 and Saffire-3 = meter-scale sample flame-spread tests in the Cygnus pressurized volume, burned to completion.
items.llmText: Saffire-1 and Saffire-3 were planned as flame spread tests of a meter-scale sample burned to completion inside the Cygnus pressurized volume.
items.note: Planned design, stated as 'planned' in the claim. Also applies to Saffire-III.

items.goldText: Saffire-II sample card: 9 samples, each 5 cm x 29 cm; materials added included SIBAL, silicone, structural PMMA, flat PMMA, PMMA with Nomex.
items.llmText: Saffire-II carried 9 samples of 5 cm x 29 cm: SIBAL, silicone, structural PMMA, flat PMMA and PMMA with Nomex.
items.note: Facts are in PSI-99, but the quote only supports the count and size; the material list comes from a different sentence and is not covered by the quote.

items.llmText: Pre-flight silicone samples for Saffire matched the NASA 6001 Test 1 geometry, 5 cm wide by 30 cm tall, in four thicknesses (0.25-1.00 mm).

items.note: 10 mm thickness is stated in the source but not inside the quote.

items.goldText: Saffire-III flow was either concurrent or opposed.
items.llmText: Saffire-III flows were either concurrent or opposed to flame spread.

items.goldText: FLEX: determine LOI as a function of ambient pressure and how a suppressant changes it.
items.llmText: A primary FLEX objective was the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) versus ambient pressure and how a suppressant changes the LOI.

items.goldText: MDCA-FLEX goal: give definition and direction for large-scale suppression tests and selection of the suppressant for next-generation crew exploration vehicles.
items.llmText: FLEX results were intended to direct large-scale fire suppression tests and the choice of fire suppressant for next-generation crew exploration vehicles.

items.goldText: Methanol droplets of ~1.5-4 mm were used so both diffusive extinction (short residence time) and radiative extinction (heat loss) occur.
items.llmText: Droplets of 1.5-4 mm were used to capture both diffusive extinction and radiative extinction.

items.goldText: ISS droplet tests: normal alkanes with NTC chemistry can burn quasi-steadily at low temperature with no visible flame.
items.llmText: ISS droplet experiments showed n-alkane fuels can sustain quasi-steady low-temperature combustion without any visible flame.

items.goldText: FLEX-2 objective 5: influence of droplet interactions on flammability limits and extinction of droplet arrays.
items.llmText: FLEX-2 studied how droplet interactions affect flammability limits and extinction of droplet arrays.

items.goldText: SAME hypothesis: in microgravity, smoke particles from pyrolyzing/smoldering sources grow larger than in 1 g (nucleation, condensation, coagulation).
items.llmText: SAME hypothesis: without buoyant flows, smoke from a pyrolyzing source grows larger particles in microgravity than in 1g.

items.goldText: Shuttle experiments confirmed that in some cases particle sizes increase in low gravity and that ISS vs shuttle detector relative performance changes; data were insufficient to design new detectors.
items.llmText: Shuttle experiments confirmed that particle sizes can increase in low gravity and that relative ISS vs shuttle detector performance changes.

items.goldText: Shuttle (ionization) and ISS (near-IR forward scattering) smoke detectors were designed without any low-gravity smoke or background-dust size data.
items.llmText: Shuttle and ISS smoke detection systems were designed without any data on low-gravity smoke or background dust size distributions.

items.llmText: SAME-R heated five spacecraft materials below ignition: Teflon, Kapton, cotton, silicone rubber and Pyrell.

items.llmText: SAME-R completed 66 test points from July 16 to September 9, 2010.

items.goldText: CFI objectives: n-dodecane and n-dodecane/iso-dodecane at 0.25-5 atm (objective 1) and helium-dilution effects (objective 2). Approach text says chamber gas 0.25-0.5 atm.

items.note: Quote supports only objective 1; helium part comes from another line. PSI-39 is internally inconsistent on the pressure range (objective 0.25-5 atm vs approach 0.25-0.5 atm); claim reports only the objective range without flagging this.

items.goldText: Cool-flame-supported quasi-steady droplet burning was first observed on ISS in the CIR with n-alkane fuels.
items.llmText: Cool-flame-supported quasi-steady droplet combustion was first observed on ISS in the Combustion Integrated Rack with n-alkane fuels.
items.note: Statement is correct, but the first observation was made in the earlier FLEX droplet tests; attaching it to CFI implies CFI discovered cool flames.

items.goldText: BRE objective 1 plans to examine NASA-considered atmospheres 14.7 psia/21%, 10.2 psia/26.5%, 8.2 psia/34%.
items.llmText: BRE examined NASA-considered crew atmospheres: 14.7 psia / 21% O2, 10.2 psia / 26.5% O2 and 8.2 psia / 34% O2.
items.note: Source says these atmospheres 'will be examined' (planned objective). The claim's past tense implies they were tested; PSI-20 does not confirm which were actually flown.

items.goldText: BRE objective: observe CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 burning on 25 and 50 mm porous burners in long-duration microgravity.
items.llmText: BRE flight tests used CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter.
items.note: Source states an objective ('Observe ...'), not a flown test matrix; claim says 'flight tests used'. 25/50 mm burners are confirmed for drop tests in NTRS 20160010073.

items.goldText: Cool diffusion flames: peak temperature 500-1000 K; discovered in 2012.
items.llmText: Cool diffusion flames have peak temperatures of 500-1000 K and were discovered in 2012.

items.goldText: Three ACME studies - soot processes, flame dynamics, low-temperature combustion - used porous spherical burners giving a nominally 1-D flame.
items.llmText: Three ACME studies (soot processes, flame dynamics, low-temperature combustion) used porous spherical burners for a nominally 1-D flame.
items.note: Source is the ACME overview, not CFI-G specific; CFI-G is the low-temperature study so attribution is reasonable.

items.goldText: Microgravity is ideal for isolating electric-field effects from buoyancy forces.
items.llmText: Microgravity isolates electric-field effects from buoyancy forces.

items.goldText: SPICE fuels: methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, propylene mixtures.
items.llmText: SPICE fuels included methane, ethylene, propane, propylene and propylene mixtures.

items.goldText: SLICE CH4 coflow flames: soot distribution shifts from centerline (1 g) to the wings (microgravity).
items.llmText: From normal gravity to microgravity, soot shifts from the flame centerline to the wings.

items.goldText: Flow-tunnel microgravity tests: 1g ULOI and 1g MOC are up to 4% O2 higher than 0g values, i.e. fuels burned in 0g at lower O2 than under NASA-STD-6001 Test 1.
items.llmText: In microgravity flow-tunnel tests, the 1g Upward Limiting Oxygen Index and Maximum Oxygen Concentration exceeded 0g values by up to 4% O2, i.e. fuels burned in 0g at lower O2 than in NASA-STD-6001 Test 1.
items.note: Not one of the 15 PSI investigations (inv = null). Source does not say the tests were in orbit (likely drop-tower); claim says 'microgravity flow-tunnel tests', which matches.

items.goldText: At 8.2 psia / 34-40% O2, material flammability is the critical hurdle: 70% of assessed subsystems need material replacements, many not yet developed.
items.llmText: In an 8.2 psia / 34-40% O2 environment, 70% of assessed ISS-heritage ECLSS subsystems would need material replacements.

outcomeAudit.method: 30 BASS rows drawn at random (Python random.Random(2026).sample over all 121 rows). The full 'Test Observations' text of each row was read and given a burn / no-burn answer for the row's initial conditions (or none when the notes do not allow one), then compared with the keyword rule. The reading was done by an AI assistant (Claude), the same model family that wrote the rules, not by an independent human annotator.

items.note: dim blue flame sustained until the fan was turned off
items.observations: difficult to ignite,very dim blue, got some soot at 16:33:51 gbx time,   N2 on at 34:18,    soot faded a bit, still have a pimple of soot,  N2 off at 34:48, fan 42:35:04, all blue flame again, like blue crescent moon.  Fan off at 35:30 ish.  Flame extinuishes right away.  Don noted no soot deposition on the sphere.  Just has bubbles.

items.note: igniter broken, no test
items.observations: Igniter seems to have broken prior to ignition.  No, 1 ohm resistance is still there.  Don trying again.  No go. A different igniter works, so igniter is broken.  No useful digital stills.

items.note: igniter broken, no test
items.observations: Igniter is broken!   Igniter inventory done.  2 good ones left.  No images taken

items.note: 'nice burn', flame reached a steady size
items.observations: nice burn, left igniter on a bit long and then on again.     Camera set to GMT, not MSG.  Appeared to reach a ss size ~ 3 cm long.

items.note: 'wake ign' and flow stepped 7.5 -> 2 cm/s imply a sustained flame, but the notes never say so explicitly
items.observations: wake ign,  3/3 initial frames before bracket.   Still camera only took initial and final set of pics, he didn't repress camera at call, he unlocked it 'reset'.  Igniter failed after this test.

items.note: all-blue flame with soot streaks
items.observations: broke igniter.    All blue with intermittent soot balls streaking back.  Might be able to get flow measurements from those.  Lab view zoomed in on flame also.

items.note: burned 2 s, died when the igniter was turned off
items.observations: Ignited and burned for only 2 s.  Died when igniter turned off.  Repeated re-ignition attempts failed.  Don didn't want it to burn since their flight suits are made of this stuff.  He felt like he should have left the igniter on longer.  Fan cal and GN2 cal  at ~16:00

items.note: ignition in 1.5 min, dim flame visible
items.observations: nice over the shoulder view, very hard to see dim flame in expt video.  Ignition in 1.5 min.

items.note: flame for ~3 min at 9 cm/s, out only when flow shut off
items.observations: (Flame from GMT 15:44:30 to 15:47:10) Ignition at 9 cm/s (FAN 60) then set FAN to 42, then slowly to 41.  After several minutes, shut flow off.  Flame became very dim blue before extinguishing.  Don’s observation: “There was a swelling action with the PMMA in which the fuel vapor coming from the sphere makes the flame swell.”

items.note: stable flame, slow downstream spread
items.observations: ignited well and had initial sooty flame wrapped around leading edge of sample.  Reduced flow to 7 cm/s and flame turned all blue -Emmons shape.  Reached a steady size and spread downstream very slowly, all blue flame.  Top stills look like about 1 cm long flame with curved base and slightly curved tail, mostly oval.   All blue with intermittent yellow streaks.   Very stable.  Spread maybe 1 cm?

items.note: went out when the igniter was retracted, twice
items.observations: tried igniting at 6 cm/s.  Flame went out when igniter was retracted, with a puff of smoke.  Tried a 2nd time, same effect.  3rd try igniter  broke/failed.  Sample showed blackened spot around mid-sample in over the shoulder view at 15:15 GMT.  Stowed igniters in bag.  Last run until January when we get new igniters up.

items.note: candle burned ~10 min
items.observations: P mode is auto-everything. Very long burn (~ 10 min), waited at every flow condition,   steady radiometer at 0.32 pot  ~ 2.2 (lowest for flame).  Consistenly goes out at pot 0.31

items.note: bright sooty flame, later blown out with N2
items.observations: ignited at 62, fan up to 87 then 100,   got long sooty tail, comet.   Envelope flame, very bright and sooty,   then fan to 42, blue LE and sooty tail.   Fan 41, slightly dimmer but still sooty tail.   Joe turned pot to 0.32 (read after) to get minimum flame (very dim blue LE only),    GN2 on max did not blow it out right away, but did eventually extinguish it.  LE blew off and ring flame stabilized for a number of s.   Card full on still camera.  Didn't seem to get the GN2 on the digital stills.  Leaving igniter in msg.  Still fuel left.

items.note: repeated ignitions, flame never sustained
items.observations: repeated ignition attempts, no luck keeping the flame sustained.  After igniter retract, the blue flame leading edge shrinks back, the tail shrinks, the flame becomes parallel to the fuel surface, and then winks out.    Apparently not flammable in opposed flow for the same concurrent flow.  Heat losses are different though, due to the metal holder around the back end of sample but not on front edge.

items.note: candle burning, out when flow stepped to 0
items.observations: Last one with over the shoulder view on this session.    Got hot then stepped to 0 flow, went out.

items.note: candle burned out all wax
items.subtypeNote: rule says flame_spread; a candle burning down is 'burned'
items.observations: same candle, 3rd test,  trying for longer time at low flow. Burned out all wax, only 2 brackets.  Flame got smaller quickly flow rates due to lack of wax.

items.note: long candle burn at low flow
items.observations: LONG candle burn at very low flow rates.  Sooty at 2 cm/s and then at 1 cm/s.   All blue at fan41.  Candle  out at flow change.

items.note: lit on 2nd try, spread around the sphere
items.observations: flame lit on 2nd try,  quickly turned sooty, spread around small remaining sphere.  All blue at lower flows, burned out fuel.  Very nice over the shoulder zoomed in view of flame.  Better than expt video!

items.note: blue flame after 3 min of attempts; out only after fan reduced
items.observations: took about 3 min to ignite, repeated attempts.  Got blue flame that was 1/2 way or mor around top.   Turned fan down in increments:12:10:20 0.6 (43); 11:15 0.5 (42); 11:50 0.35 (41) and 12:35 0.32 (41)   flame self-extinguished.

items.note: flame blown out by N2, so it was burning
items.observations: flame did blow out with GN2 at about a pot 6.

items.note: ignited in 1 min, symmetric growth
items.observations: Ign in 1 min.  Symmetric growth.  Gets sooty, even when flow reduced to 41.  Gets all blue at 18:38, out at 18:40 at finite extremely low flow.

items.note: burned on the forward stagnation region, minimal spread
items.subtypeNote: rule says flame_spread; notes say 'minimal spread', 'burned' fits better
items.observations: broke 2 igniters on this trying to get it to ignite. 3rd one was suspect, and didn't work.  2nd vitiation, got it ignited, burned just on forward stagnation region, minimal spread.  Went out at finite flow.  Post burn shape was crater and protrusion on lower half.

items.note: candle ran out of fuel
items.observations: higher flow test, but ran out of fuel too quickly.

items.note: did not ignite, igniter on the whole test
items.observations: leave igniter on entire test to provide additional heat to flame.  Did not ignite.  Not even any smoke.  Flow too high?

items.note: sooty bullet-shaped flame, out when fan off
items.observations: ignited at 10 cm/s, fan to 42,   less vapor jetting noted, bullet shaped flame, sooty.   Fan to 41, similar, slightly smaller flame.    Fan off flame all blue and pulses a few times before extinguished.  Jay saw cloud go by when he turned on fan at GMT 17:12 ish.

items.note: steady spreading
items.observations: Nice symmetric burn, some soot at 10 cm/s,  Steady spreading, flame seems to reach a steady length.  Decreasing flow shrinks flame and changes to mostly blue, but still spreading.  Gets very dim near end of sample as it shrinks and extinguishes at burnout.  Don noted the fiberglass matrix was still intact after the burn.

items.note: ignited nicely, sooty flame
items.observations: first wax slab test.   Ignited nicely.  Very sooty flame wrapped around leading edge.  Turned flow down to 3 cm/s.  Flame sooty for a while, then as it burned out leading edge it got dimmer, shorter and eventully  all blue.  Shrank slowly and extinguished by itself.

items.note: burning laminar, very fast burning rate
items.observations: Burning laminar but sooty at 42, turned down very slowly to 41 and flame started to turn blue and vapor jet.  Turned fan to max, and flame did not blow off stagnation region.  Burning rate incredibly fast.  Turned off flow right when fuel completely ran out.  Don examined igniter and there is one thin spot, so may not last much longer.

items.note: dim blue flame spreading upwind
items.observations: No Don camera.  Wake flame very dim on video, all blue, spread very slowly upwind.  Ignited GBX time 16:14:44,  N2 on at 16:17:18,  did not extinguish, increased to pot 10, at 16:18:37,  N2 off at 16:19:19.  Accidentaly turned fan up briefly instead of N2.  Fan turned to 40 at 16:19:22, flame and flame went out at 16:19:34.  All times GBX.

items.note: flame spread on the top side, out with flow off
items.observations: Ignited and turned flow down, then N2 on while flame was small and blue.    Flame did not go out completely, but only seemed to spread on the top side of the video view.  It wrapped around quite far on top, but not quite to stag. Region.  Turned N2 off and flame grew and got sottier.  Extinguished with flow off at6.75 minutes or so.  Joe asked about why N2 didn't put out flame.
